subtitle: Little words of contracts, and describing words that take a case
words.intro: Every German contract has a language of its own, and it’s older than the people who sign it. Learn twelve little words, and you can read your lease, your insurance and, if you must, a judgment from Karlsruhe.

grammar[0].fact: The Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe has the last word on German politics. The Basic Law’s first article is on a glass wall by the Spree in Berlin, and it begins: *Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar.* It’s one of the best-known sentences in the language.

document.intro: A real article of the Basic Law, cut into glass by the Bundestag in Berlin. Two short sentences, each with a passive and a promise. *Unverletzlich* can’t be broken; *auf Grund eines Gesetzes* is the small door left open.
document.fact: The Basic Law’s first nineteen articles are the basic rights, and they cannot lightly be changed. The first one, on human dignity, cannot be changed at all. Citizens may take a complaint about them to Karlsruhe at no cost.

reading.intro: Max has been given his first proper contract, and he has signed it without reading it. Now he’s asked a lawyer, Frau Dr. Kranz, who happens to be Lena’s aunt. She’s reading it at Sunday lunch, and she has stopped eating.
reading.photos[1].caption: Ein Kanzleischild, durchgestrichen: So beendete man 1933 die Arbeit jüdischer Anwälte.
reading.fact: German employment law protects you against a great deal, including your own signature: a clause that’s unfair or surprising in small print, an *überraschende Klausel*, simply doesn’t count. So many German contracts run for pages and a judge throws out several of them.
